stories.headline: Newsom's bid to empty California's death row collides with voters' repeated rejection of abolition
stories.note: Newsom is defying California voters who have repeatedly rejected abolishing the death penalty, a soft-on-crime contrast for the 2028 hopeful.
body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom said on Nov. 5 that he plans to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the state's death row to life in prison without parole, once the required legal steps are done.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation has now asked the California Supreme Court to block the move. Its suit says Newsom skipped required notice to district attorneys, bypassed the Board of Parole Hearings referral the Legislature requires, and ignored victims' families' right to be notified and heard. The coalition behind it includes law enforcement leaders, victims' rights groups and several DAs, among them Sacramento County DA Thien Ho, a Democrat.

Opponents point out that Californians have voted to keep capital punishment twice: they defeated Proposition 34 in 2012 and Proposition 62 in 2016. Heritage Foundation legal fellow Zack Smith told Fox News Digital that Newsom is effectively using clemency to override that verdict and substitute his own view.

CJLF president Anne Marie Schubert called it a defense of victims and the rule of law, saying "blanket commutation is not an exercise of discretion — it is an abandonment of it." Some of the state's most notorious serial killers are among the inmates affected. Neither CJLF nor Newsom's office responded to Fox's request for comment.
Why it matters: Newsom is a likely 2028 Democratic contender, and a mass commutation that runs against voters' repeated choices hands Republicans a clear soft-on-crime contrast.

stories.headline: Jeffries calling Jerusalem NYC's ‘sixth borough’ resurfaces as progressives swing against Israel
stories.note: Jeffries' old remark puts him in a squeeze as his party's left flank turns on Israel, exposing a Democratic rift.
body: A 2020 clip of House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries telling an AIPAC audience that New Yorkers consider Jerusalem "the 6th Borough" has gone viral again, just after he secured his party's nomination for speaker.

In the interview, Jeffries joked he was visiting Israel a fifth time to "catch up with my constituents," and described Israel as living in a tough neighborhood surrounded by Hamas, Hezbollah, Syria and a nuclear-minded Iran.

The resurfaced remarks land as the progressive wing of his party, and some establishment members, increasingly condemn AIPAC and break from traditional U.S. support for Israel. That raises the question of how far Jeffries will bend to calls for a tougher look at the U.S.-Israel relationship.
Jeffries won the caucus's secret-ballot vote 251 to 11, but he still needs a simple majority of the full 435-member House in January's floor vote to become speaker.
Why it matters: Israel is becoming a wedge inside the Democratic Party, and its incoming House leader is caught between his own record and an increasingly hostile left flank.

stories.headline: NYC college put on notice after Jewish campus group shunned by student government: 'rude awakening'
stories.note: Another campus antisemitism flashpoint in New York keeps pressure on progressive institutions.
body: Hunter College's undergraduate student government, part of the CUNY system, canceled a "Cultural Arts Night" after other student groups objected to the school's Hillel chapter taking part, according to the New York Post. Students for Justice in Palestine reportedly helped plan the event.
The college itself acknowledged to the Post that some groups pulled out because Hunter Hillel planned to participate. Protesters rallied outside the school on Nov. 19.

Activist Shabbos Kestenbaum, who works for PragerU, called it "blatant anti-Jewish discrimination" and noted the event had no problem including groups tied to countries with far worse records until a Jewish group joined. He argues the school may have violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, which bars discrimination by institutions receiving federal funds.
The student government apologized, saying the event "should never have moved forward" and pledging to keep such a mistake from happening again.
Why it matters: Another campus antisemitism blowup in New York keeps public universities, and the progressive activism around them, under scrutiny that Republicans have pressed for years.

stories.headline: How a $1B Obama-era solar plant went bankrupt twice, leaving taxpayers with the tab
stories.note: A costly green-energy flop from the Obama years reinforces the GOP case against Democrats' subsidy spending.
body: The Crescent Dunes solar plant near Tonopah, Nevada, backed by more than $1 billion in federal support under the Obama administration, has gone bankrupt a second time and sold for just $7 million. The estimated cost to taxpayers could reach about $507.6 million.

The project got a $737 million federal loan guarantee and roughly $275 million in Treasury grants. Its 640-foot tower and 10,000-plus mirrors were meant to heat molten salt and keep generating power after dark, with the Energy Department projecting enough peak output for more than 75,000 homes.

After it opened in late 2015, leaks and equipment failures kept knocking it offline, output fell short and cheaper solar undercut it. The late Sen. Harry Reid had hailed it in 2016 as an "engineering and clean energy marvel."
The potential loss nearly matches the $528 million taxpayers lost on Solyndra. Rep. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, called the project "a microcosm of what is wrong with Democrat governance."
Why it matters: It's a fresh, concrete example for Republicans arguing that Democrats' green-energy subsidies gamble taxpayer money on projects that don't deliver.

stories.headline: Trump orders federal contractors to alert White House on congressional record requests
stories.note: Trump moves to get ahead of incoming House Democrats' investigations before they can blindside the administration.
body: President Trump signed an executive order late Friday requiring all federal contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House when Congress asks them for information, and to hold back material the administration considers privileged. Companies that don't comply could lose contracts or be barred from future work.

The order says lawmakers have been "harassing private companies" to pry loose confidential executive branch information. It follows a directive this week from White House Counsel Will Scharf telling agencies to clear employee testimony to Congress with the administration first.

Democrats, who won both chambers in the midterms, plan to probe the administration, the Trump family's business dealings, immigration enforcement and the Epstein files. Likely Oversight chair Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., has already sent preservation letters to 12 current and former officials, including VP JD Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump and Stephen Miller.

Critics call the moves an effort to shield the executive branch from oversight, and the order could draw legal challenges if contractors are told to withhold subpoenaed records, since courts can step into those fights.
Why it matters: The White House is getting ahead of the coming wave of Democratic investigations instead of waiting to be put on defense.

stories.headline: Trump says Vance, Rubio are 'doing fantastically' ahead of 2028 Republican presidential primary
stories.note: Trump talks up a strong GOP bench for 2028 with Vance and Rubio both in good standing.
body: On Fox News' "Saturday in America," President Trump told host Kayleigh McEnany that Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are "doing fantastically" and are "both very, very popular" heading toward 2028.
Trump said other capable Republicans could also emerge. Names floated include Sen. Ted Cruz, Gov. Ron DeSantis, Mike Pence, Brian Kemp and Glenn Youngkin.
On the Democratic side, he said Kamala Harris and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez seem to be doing well, but predicted Democrats may end up with someone nobody has heard of.

Asked whether the GOP should hold an open primary or rally behind a unity ticket, Trump said it could be either, adding that a unity ticket saves money that can be used "against the Democrats." He said the party will be "involved" whoever the nominee is.
Why it matters: Trump is signaling confidence in a deep Republican bench while Democrats still lack a clear front-runner.

stories.headline: Apex predator at center of farmers vs environmentalists fight as Trump weighs major move: 'Out of control'
stories.note: Trump weighs siding with farmers and ranchers over environmental groups, a winning issue in rural America.
body: The Interior Department has until Dec. 3 to decide whether gray wolves and Mexican wolves have met Endangered Species Act recovery criteria. If they have, the department must start removing or easing federal protections, a step that could affect Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, California and Colorado.

Minnesota farmer Shayne Isane, who has nearly 300 cattle, told Fox News Digital he's lost calves to wolves, including three in one night, and can't legally shoot them even while they attack his herd. He says the population is "out of control" and state-recommended deterrents haven't worked.

Environmentalists oppose delisting, warning it could bring culling, trapping and trophy hunting. The Minnesota DNR estimates about 2,400 wolves in the state and calls the population stable, not rapidly growing.

White House deputy press secretary Taylor Rogers said the Biden administration's "radical environmental policies" left ranchers defenseless. Interior said it had no update yet but recognizes the challenges wolves pose to livestock producers.
Why it matters: Siding with farmers and ranchers over environmental groups is a popular stance in rural America and keeps the GOP's contrast with Biden-era policy front and center.
